newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia says not blocking foreign investors.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia says not blocking foreign investors.

text.p: The Bank of Slovenia on Friday defended new regulations that force international investors to open special share trading accounts and reiterated its goal was to regulate foreign investment and not block it.
"Foreigners want to know under what conditions they can participate in our market and it is right that we tell them at the start," Bank of Slovenia governor France Arhar told a news conference.
Last week the bank ruled that foreign investors must hold special accounts, called custody accounts, at any of Slovenia's 14 fully licensed banks if they wanted to buy shares.
New investors must open the accounts from Monday. Investors that already own Slovenian shares have 30 days from February 7.
The central bank estimated that foreign portfolio investors had invested some $60 million in Slovenian securities, with a rapid increase in the inflow of funds from the end of September.

"The central bank has to regulate foreign financial transactions due to the lack of proper legislation. For example, there is no law on mergers and acquisitions," Arhar said, adding that the new accounts brought Slovenia into line with other countries.
Slovenian banks said they would need two weeks to prepare for the accounts.
The stock exchanged criticised the central bank's information policy, claiming inadequate information was behind a sharp fall in Slovenian share prices this week.
"Our financial market is so sensitive that it can be significantly influenced by any information which is not detailed enough," said Drasko Veselinovic, head of the Ljubljana bourse.
"We support the establishment of the accounts but believe the central bank should inform everybody at the same time," he added.

The central bank notified some Slovenian banks of the new decree last Friday afternoon, while others claimed they only received the news on Monday afternoon. The national bank called its first news conference on the matter a week later.
On Tuesday, when information of the new decree spread, the SBI index fell 8.46 percent to 1,521.8. By Thursday it was down to 1,295.2 points but managed to regain 5.72 percent on Friday.

"The panic is over, but there will be no fresh foreign capital until custody accounts are established, therefore volumes and prices may fall next week," an analyst said. -- Marja Novak, Ljubljana newsroom, 386-61-125-8439
